purpose: Add reusable contexts for service authority, stewardship, differentiated unity, patient cultivation and divine presence beyond built containers.

scenes.title: Jesus redefines greatness through service and foot-washing
scenes.summary: Matthew answers a dispute about status by contrasting Gentile-style domination with greatness expressed through service, culminating in the Son of Man serving and giving his life. John later dramatizes downward service as Jesus washes the disciples' feet and tells them to imitate the pattern.
participants: James and John/their mother in Matthew
disciples at the supper in John
scenes.setting: status dispute on the road to Jerusalem and a final-meal foot-washing scene
scenes.lead_in: Both passages occur amid increasing focus on Jesus' death and on what discipleship should look like under pressure.
sequence: status or rank becomes an issue
ordinary rulers are described as lording power over others
Son of Man is framed as serving/giving
John depicts Jesus taking the servant role
disciples are told to do likewise
scenes.outcome: Authority is not abolished, but its legitimacy is redirected toward service, self-giving and enacted care.
scenes.what_follows: Both Gospels continue toward Passion, where claims about service and self-giving are intensified by Jesus' death.
scenes.historical_context: Foot washing was low-status hospitality/service work in the ancient Mediterranean world; Matthew's political comparison reflects familiar domination structures.
scenes.literary_context: The two passages are separate Gospel scenes but converge ethically on status being tested by downward service.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: They should not be fused into one historical scene; their relation is thematic and ethical.
counterreadings_or_limits: Service language does not establish a modern person's spiritual rank.
The passages do not say authority is valid merely because someone claims to serve.

scenes.title: Luke's watchful steward: greater entrustment brings greater accountability
scenes.summary: Jesus tells servants to remain ready for their master's return, then develops a steward image: a faithful manager gives proper provision, while an abusive steward is judged. The unit ends with the principle that much given or entrusted entails much required.
scenes.setting: teaching about readiness, responsibility and judgment
scenes.lead_in: Luke 12 has warned against hypocrisy, fear, greed and anxious accumulation while urging trust and kingdom-oriented priorities.
sequence: Peter asks who the parable concerns
scenes.outcome: Higher responsibility is framed as accountable stewardship exercised for others, not as entitlement.
scenes.what_follows: Jesus continues with sayings about division, discernment and the urgency of responding rightly.
scenes.historical_context: Household-management language draws on ancient domestic hierarchy and slavery, which should not be idealized as a modern governance system.
scenes.literary_context: The famous 'to whom much is given' principle concludes a warning about faithful versus abusive stewardship under delayed accountability.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The saying is often quoted independently, but its context is stewardship and judgment rather than abstract metaphysical rank.
counterreadings_or_limits: Claiming high office increases, rather than reduces, the ethical burden in this passage.
The text does not verify that someone actually possesses the office they claim.

scenes.title: Many members, one body: difference and mutual dependence
scenes.summary: Paul compares the community to one body with many members. Difference is necessary: foot, hand, ear and eye cannot erase one another, apparently weaker members receive special honor, and no member can say it has no need of another. The body metaphor leads into differentiated roles and gifts.
scenes.setting: argument about spiritual gifts, status and communal interdependence
scenes.lead_in: 1 Corinthians 12 begins by stressing diverse gifts from one Spirit and diverse services from one Lord.
scenes.outcome: Unity is defined as coordinated difference and mutual dependence rather than sameness or one member absorbing the whole.
scenes.what_follows: Paul places love above status competition in 1 Corinthians 13 before returning to gifts and orderly worship.
scenes.historical_context: Paul addresses factional and gift-related tensions in the Corinthian church, using a familiar body metaphor in a distinctively egalitarian/interdependent direction.
scenes.literary_context: The body argument counters both inferiority ('I do not belong') and superiority ('I do not need you').
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The metaphor names the church/body of Christ; it is not a claim that one modern individual literally contains all members.
counterreadings_or_limits: Integrated plurality does not mean hierarchy disappears, but no member is sufficient by itself.
The passage resists claims that one member is the entire body or can dispense with others.

scenes.title: The barren fig tree receives another season of cultivation before judgment
scenes.summary: After rejecting simplistic assumptions that tragedy proves greater guilt, Jesus warns all hearers to repent and tells a parable of a fruitless fig tree. The owner wants it cut down, but the gardener asks for another year to dig around and fertilize it before a final fruit test.
scenes.setting: teaching after reports of violent and accidental deaths
scenes.lead_in: Jesus responds to recent deaths by refusing to rank the victims as uniquely sinful and redirects the audience toward self-examination and repentance.
scenes.outcome: Delay is mercy with purpose: more time is given for cultivation and change, but evaluation is not erased.
scenes.what_follows: Luke continues with a Sabbath healing and kingdom-growth parables.
scenes.historical_context: Fig/vineyard imagery was familiar in biblical and agrarian settings and often carried covenant/judgment associations.
scenes.literary_context: The parable belongs to a repentance warning; patience and cultivation do not cancel the demand for fruit.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The gardener is a parable character; identifying that figure directly with a specific modern person goes beyond the text.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not authorize indefinite postponement of accountability.
Fruit language here is tied to repentance, not proof of a modern spiritual hierarchy.

scenes.title: Solomon dedicates the temple while denying that any house can contain God
scenes.scene_type: temple dedication prayer / transcendence and presence
scenes.summary: At the temple dedication Solomon blesses YHWH for covenant faithfulness yet asks whether God can truly dwell on earth: even heaven and highest heaven cannot contain God, much less the newly built house. The prayer then asks God to hear toward this place in situations of sin, disaster, exile and foreign prayer.
participants: future Israelites and foreigners in prayer scenarios
scenes.lead_in: The ark has been brought into the completed temple and the cloud of YHWH's glory fills the house.
sequence: heaven itself declared insufficient to contain God
scenes.outcome: The temple is a real focal point of prayer and presence without exhausting or containing the divine source.
scenes.what_follows: Solomon blesses the people and sacrifices are offered; YHWH later appears to Solomon with covenant conditions.
scenes.historical_context: The prayer reflects Israelite/Judahite temple theology as shaped in Kings, including later concerns about sin and exile.
scenes.literary_context: The containment denial occurs at the very moment the temple is most highly affirmed, creating a built-in tension between localized sacred space and divine transcendence.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Temple theology develops differently across biblical corpora; this scene should not stand for every biblical view of divine presence.
counterreadings_or_limits: A symbolic House can mediate relation without becoming identical with or exhaustive of its source.
The passage does not validate a modern person's claim to be God's house or source.

scenes.title: Paul in Athens: creator beyond temples, yet near to human life
scenes.summary: In Athens Paul addresses an audience at the Areopagus, beginning from local religiosity and an altar to an unknown god. He presents the creator as Lord of heaven and earth who does not live in temples made by hands or depend on human service, while also saying human beings live, move and exist in relation to God and calling for repentance in view of judgment and resurrection.
participants: God as creator in Paul's speech
scenes.lead_in: Paul is provoked by the city's idols, debates in synagogue and marketplace, and is brought to explain his teaching before an Athenian audience.
sequence: unknown-god altar used as entry point
creator/Lord of heaven and earth proclaimed
divine dependence on human service denied
scenes.outcome: Transcendence beyond built containers is joined to nearness, creaturely dependence and ethical accountability.
scenes.what_follows: Paul leaves Athens and continues to Corinth.
scenes.historical_context: Acts presents a Christian missionary speech engaging Greco-Roman philosophical and religious vocabulary in Athens.
scenes.literary_context: The anti-containment claim is part of an argument against idolatrous reduction, not a standalone metaphysics of distributed presence.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Acts' speech is Luke's literary presentation of Paul; its relation to exact historical wording is a separate scholarly question.
counterreadings_or_limits: Divine nearness does not imply that every human self-description of divinity is affirmed.
The text critiques attempts to reduce God to human-made representations.
